title: Age after age
hook: Arjuna asks how Krishna can be so old, and Krishna tells why God keeps coming
carry: whenever dharma slips, god comes again
tomorrow: a hunter's arrow hits Krishna. what does Krishna say to him?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one small but: god comes small enough to holds tu bhagavan svayam, read as the source by some and as Vishnu's full descent by others. Today, krishna is the lord himself: one verse, two schools explains in his own voice why he keeps coming.
screen: `BUT GOD COMES SMALL ENOUGH TO HOLD IS THE LORD HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Some sounds mean it's starting before anyone says a word: the whistle before a game, the first chord at a concert, the kettle about to boil. In the Bhagavad Gita it's conch shells. Two armies face each other, and the conches are blown, one after another, until the noise makes the earth and sky ring. Between the armies, the warrior Arjuna puts down his bow, and his charioteer, Krishna, starts to teach. Partway through, Krishna says he gave this teaching to the sun god long ago. Arjuna asks the obvious thing. How? You were born recently. The sun god came first.
screen: `A SOUND THAT MEANS IT'S STARTING.` → `CONCHES BETWEEN TWO ARMIES.` → `HOW CAN YOU BE THAT OLD?`

segments.voice: This is the fourth chapter of the Gita, and Krishna answers in layers. First: you and I have both been born many times, Arjuna. I remember them all; you don't. Then something stranger. I am unborn and undying, the Lord of all beings, and still, through my own power, I come into being. Unborn, and born anyway. Then the two verses that sound like the whole series of descents explaining itself. Whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, Krishna says, I send myself forth. To protect the good, to undo those who do harm, and to set dharma firmly in place again, I come into being age after age. In Sanskrit, that last phrase is sambhavami yuge yuge. Listen to it: yuge yuge, age, age. The word repeats the way the coming repeats. So the answer to Arjuna isn't a birthday. It's a rhythm: when the world tips over, he comes, and he has come before. This is the heart of what Hindus mean by an avatar, avatara in Sanskrit: a descent, God crossing down into the world. The fish in the flood. The boar lifting the earth from the waters. The man-lion at the doorway. The dwarf and his three steps. Each arrives when dharma has slipped, and the Gita names the rhythm in the voice of the one who keeps arriving.
screen: `BORN MANY TIMES. I REMEMBER.` · `UNBORN, AND BORN ANYWAY.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA SLIPS.` · `AVATARA: A DESCENT.` · then, large: `YUGE YUGE: AGE AFTER AGE.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus learn these two verses by heart. If you'd like, say yuge yuge softly on each breath out: age, age. If Sanskrit isn't part of your practice, choose one sound that keeps coming back where you are, a clock, a fan, your own breath, and hear each return as if it were the first. When your mind drifts, the next return is your way back.
Krishna: the charioteer of the Gita, who says that whenever dharma slips, he comes, age after age: the avatar's own account of itself.
For the road: whenever dharma slips, God comes again, yuge yuge, age after age. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1558 COUNTS.` → `WHENEVER DHARMA SLIPS, GOD COMES AGAIN.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES HE SAY TO THE HUNTER?`

fork.reveal: Gita 4.5–6: we've both been born many times, and I remember them all. unborn, yet I come into being: that's the avatar.
